title: Influences and the Joe Henderson period
summary: Jackson traces his listening from Parker, Dexter Gordon and Sonny Rollins to Joe Henderson, whose influence took him years to dilute.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Coleman Hawkins and the great saxophonists

blocks.x: Probably someone has asked you in the past about your grounding, of those artists. Who do you feel you sort of came out of?

Well I like to say I steal from everybody. I mean well the original obviously would be Charlie Parker, because someone said, that’s where you start. My father was giving me Gene Ammons and Sonny Stitt records so I was listening to that, then came Charlie Parker, then someone said well you need to listen to Dexter Gordon, then I went to see him, then somebody said well okay now you’ve got to check out a guy named Sonny Rollins. Okay you’ve got Sonny Rollins, okay, what about Lucky Thompson. Okay, what about Coleman Hawkins. Then you’re all over the place. Then after a while Joe Henderson comes along for me, which was a biggie for me. Then all of a sudden I find a guy named Eddie Harris, and so I started listening to him. Well then all of a sudden you say well let’s move to the trumpet. And then you hear a guy named Freddie Hubbard. Then you listen to the trombone and you’ve got J.J. Johnson. Well let’s go to the bass, you’ve got Paul Chambers. And I’ve learned things from all those musicians. I didn’t even mention Miles, how much I learned from him. So there’s so much that’s available to us. You just listen, and if you enjoy it you try to figure it out a little bit and see what you can use from it and at the same point, as you become an older person, you will find your own way of delivering it. Some people can do it quicker than others. Some people are able to get to it at 19 or 20. But sometimes you have to live a long time, or live a while before you can play something that, you know what, I’m going to play this, this is what I want to play. And you feel comfortable with doing that, and you feel good about it, as opposed to man, I did that but Coltrane wouldn’t have done that. You see when you get to a certain age and confidence level you’re okay with the fact that Coltrane did it this way and I’m going to do it my way, because we’re both, at the end of the day, doing the same thing, we’re trying to just enjoy ourselves. But it takes a period, for some, of development. It took me a period, longer probably than others, where I really felt like, you know, this is the way Javon feels about it and I didn’t feel like I had to be just like Joe Henderson where there was a period where I really was — I won’t say obsessed because I didn’t stalk him — but I really was listening to all his recordings and then after a while it started to be to a point where everybody would say oh man he sounds like Joe Henderson. Well it got to a point where it just wasn’t flattering anymore. It used to be

flattering, but it got to a point, it didn’t hurt my feelings but at a certain point where I said wow, there’s other things in there than just Joe Henderson. But for whatever reason, people heard that and you still, again, you just keep building and try to go through the wall. And after a while you let some other influences come into my life and the fact of the matter was there was a lot of Joe Henderson paid attention to by me. And so once I started letting some other things seep through, some other styles, some other ideas, then it started to dilute itself a little bit. It’s still there, but it diluted itself.
